name: Ebisu East Park Public Toilet
tagline: Fumihiko Maki's thin white roof floats above the park—locals call it the Squid.
description:
Fumihiko Maki's contribution to the Tokyo Toilet Project sits in a small Ebisu park better known for its octopus-shaped play slide. His response was deceptively quiet: a thin white roof, gently curved at the edges, hovering above three small volumes—men's, women's and a universal stall—arranged around an open central courtyard. From above the roof spreads its tentacle-like extensions over a bench seat, an information board and the entrances, earning the building its nickname: the Squid.

The move is generosity disguised as restraint. By breaking the programme into separate volumes and slipping a courtyard between them, Maki removes the conventional toilet building's sense of enclosure. Sightlines stay open through the structure, the bench invites loitering, and the accessible stall sits visible from the street rather than hidden in a corner. It's a quiet argument that a public restroom can simply be public space with plumbing.

visitorTips.title: Getting There
visitorTips.description: Five minutes' walk from Ebisu Station's East Exit; the park sits just behind the Yebisu Garden Place approach.

visitorTips.title: Best Time
visitorTips.description: Daytime, when the white roof catches the light and the courtyard is open to the sky.

visitorTips.title: Good to Know
visitorTips.description: Combine with the Yoyogi-Fukamachi Transparent Toilet and Jingu-Dori Amayadori for a Tokyo Toilet Project mini-tour.

visitorTips.title: Accessibility
visitorTips.description: Universal stall with grab rails, ostomate fixtures and a wall-mounted child seat.

name: Modern Kawaya at Ebisu Park
tagline: Fifteen concrete walls scattered like neolithic huts—Wonderwall's love letter to the original Japanese kawaya.
description:
Masamichi Katayama of Wonderwall called his Tokyo Toilet entry 'Modern Kawaya'—a reference to the ambiguous, semi-public squat-shelters that Japanese villagers improvised from rocks, branches and walls long before plumbing arrived. His version sets fifteen randomly-rotated concrete walls in a small Ebisu park, threaded by passages that lead the visitor inward to the stalls and washbasins at the centre.

The arrangement deliberately resists the conventional restroom block. From outside it reads as a small civic sculpture; from inside the walls open and close around you, framing fragments of trees and sky. Board-formed concrete gives way to warmer interior surfaces—proof that even a programme as banal as a public toilet can survive being treated as architecture.

visitorTips.title: Getting There
visitorTips.description: Three minutes' walk from Ebisu Station West Exit, on the eastern edge of Ebisu Park.

visitorTips.title: Best Time
visitorTips.description: Late afternoon, when long shadows accentuate the walls' irregular geometry.

visitorTips.title: Good to Know
visitorTips.description: The fifteen-wall arrangement is best appreciated by walking the full perimeter before stepping inside.

visitorTips.title: Accessibility
visitorTips.description: Wheelchair-accessible universal stall with full fixtures.

name: The House at Jingumae
tagline: NIGO's small cottage with a red roof—a quiet nod to the Washington Heights houses that once stood nearby.
description:
When NIGO (Tomoaki Nagao, founder of A Bathing Ape and now creative director of Kenzo) was asked to design a public toilet, he reached past architectural vocabulary to a piece of neighbourhood history: the Washington Heights houses. From 1946 to 1964 the area now occupied by Yoyogi Park and the surrounding Jingumae blocks was an American military housing compound—rows of pitched-roof cottages in mint and white that became, for many Japanese, an early visual shorthand for postwar America.

The restroom takes that cottage form almost literally. A red-shingled gable roof sits over white clapboard walls trimmed in mint blue; inside, exposed white trusses run beneath the vaulted ceiling and a picket-fence partition lets daylight wash across the urinals. It is, in NIGO's hands, almost a Pop-art gesture—the toilet as a fragment of Tokyo's appropriated mid-century imagery, dropped back onto its original site.

visitorTips.title: Getting There
visitorTips.description: A few minutes' walk from Meiji-Jingumae 'Harajuku' Station or Yoyogi-Hachiman Station.

visitorTips.title: Best Time
visitorTips.description: Mid-morning, when daylight filters through the mint picket-fence partition.

visitorTips.title: Good to Know
visitorTips.description: Read up on Washington Heights (1946–1964) before visiting—it adds a layer to the cottage form.

visitorTips.title: Accessibility
visitorTips.description: Universal stall with washlet, sink and grab rails.
